extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle scholars, general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Aristotle's evaluative criteria for friendship and related duties from Book IX of the Nicomachean Ethics, including types of friendship, grounds for dissolution, obligations to relatives/benefactors, and notions of self-love and unity of sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate equality in dissimilar friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: In all the Friendships the parties to which are dissimilar it is the proportionate which equalises and preserves the Friendship; e.g. the cobbler gets an equivalent for his shoes after a certain rate; a common measure has been provided in money, and to this accordingly all things are referred and by this are measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties are dissimilar, a proportionate equivalent (often money) is the measure that equalises relations; disputes arise when the parties aim at different objects (pleasure vs gain). Examples include tradesmen exchanging goods/services at a rate. If intentions differ, dealings cannot be fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship based on pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship of the lover for the beloved object is based upon pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such friendships are liable to break when the pleasurable qualities cease; the lover may love qualities (not the person) that are not permanent, so the friendship is not lasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship based on utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship of the other (non-lover) for him is based upon utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These friendships depend on usefulness and tend to end when the utility ceases; they are not grounded in disinterested regard and thus are not permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship based on moral character (virtue) is permanent
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship based upon the moral character of the parties, being independent and disinterested, is permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the highest form of friendship: it is stable because it is grounded in the goodness of the persons themselves rather than transient pleasures or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate requital should refer to the giver's intention
rubrics_metrics.description: The requital is to be made with reference to the intention of the other, the intention being characteristic of the true friend and of goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If first services were given disinterestedly, the first giver should not later demand exact equivalent; requital should respect the spirit of the original act. When no stipulation is made, those who gave first disinterestedly are not expected to raise the question of exact repayment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified reward implies contentment ('With specified reward a friend should be content')
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reward is specified in advance, a friend should accept that specification and be content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who take money in advance and then perform nothing are blameworthy (e.g., Sophists who take fees and do not deliver). The maxim supports honoring explicit agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the receiver should fix value
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the original giving is avowedly for some return, then for the receiver to fix the value would seem not only necessary but also fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiver-estimation is fair because the first giver has already enjoyed the pleasure/benefit; the receiver should estimate value not by current post-acquisition valuation but by what he set upon it before he obtained it. Laws sometimes avoid actions on voluntary dealings on similar principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of obligations varies by relation (parents, benefactors, companions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions arise whether one's father has an unlimited claim on one's services, or whether the sick man is to obey his physician; the claims of parents, brothers, companions, and benefactors are all different and one must give to each what belongs to and befits each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single person can unite all claims; obligations must be discriminated according to amount, what is honourable, and what is necessary. For example, maintenance and assistance are typically owed to parents in preference to others, but not all kinds of honour are due to parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requital of benefits generally higher duty than unsolicited kindnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The requital of benefits is, in general, a higher duty than doing unsolicited kindnesses to one's companion; discharging a debt is more obligatory than giving to a companion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions may apply when giving is far more honourable or necessary than repayment; moral context can override the default priority of debt repayment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions where giving outweighs repayment (honour/necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a particular case the giving greatly preponderates as being either honourable or necessary, we must be swayed by these considerations even if a debt exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ransoming a father might take precedence; obligations can be unequal if one party acted under different beliefs about the recipient's character (good vs scoundrel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution of friendships based on utility or pleasure when motives cease
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of those whose motive to Friendship is utility or pleasure there can be nothing wrong in breaking up the connection when they no longer have those qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is reasonable for such friendships to cease when their foundations (pleasure/utility) vanish. However, deception—pretending to be friends for virtue when really for utility—is blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deception about grounds of friendship is blameworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: A man has reason to find fault if the other party, being really attached because of advantage or pleasure, pretended to be so because of his moral character; he has a right to find fault—indeed more than with utterers of false coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretence of virtue in friendship is a kind of moral shamming; the deceived party may justly reproach the pretender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to help friends improve morally versus severance
rubrics_metrics.description: When one party remains what he was while the other becomes morally improved, if there is a chance of amendment in the depraved friend we are bound to aid in repairing the moral character of our friends even more than their substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking off is not necessarily wrong but should be reserved for incurable depravity; if improvement is possible, the virtuous response is to assist moral reform rather than immediately sever ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindly Feeling is distinct from Friendship and is a starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: Kindly Feeling, though resembling Friendship, is not identical with it, because it may exist regarding those we do not know and without the object being aware of it; it does not imply the intensity or yearning of Affection and may arise suddenly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kindly Feeling is a 'dormant Friendship'—it can ripen into true Friendship if it endures and develops into intimacy, but often it remains superficial and does not prompt joint action or sacrifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Sentiment (social Friendship) concerns shared aims in action
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Sentiment has for its object matters of action, and such of these as are of importance and of mutual interest; it is plainly a social Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of Sentiment is not mere Unity of Opinion (which can exist among strangers on theoretical points). It involves agreement on expediency and joint commitment to common action (e.g., choosing magistrates or alliances). It characteristically exists among the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefactors often have more friendship for beneficiaries than vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefactors are commonly held to have more Friendship for the objects of their kindness than these for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations: benefactors are 'creators' of a sort and value what cost them labour; they derive honour and lasting pleasure from their act (the work abides), while recipients enjoy transient advantage. Also, favourers may expect requital but recipients may not feel equivalent affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: People value more what cost them labour; creators love their works
rubrics_metrics.description: All people value most what has cost them much labour in the production; artisans and poets especially feel affection for their work as if it were their children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This natural attachment explains why benefactors care more for beneficiaries (the beneficiary is akin to the benefactor's 'work'). It affects direction and magnitude of friendly feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-love: the reproached kind (selfish) vs the proper, virtuous self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: The reproached kind of 'Self-loving' denotes those who give themselves the larger share of wealth, honours, and bodily pleasures (associated with the mass of mankind). By contrast, the virtuous man loves and gratifies the intellectual principle (Reason) and is therefore truly Self-loving in a noble sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-love is blameworthy when it privileges base goods and passions; it is praiseworthy when it means cherishing the rational principle and securing noble goods (virtue). The virtuous man's self-love results in acting for honourable ends and benefits the community if others emulate such self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good men can be friends with themselves; wicked men cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: The good man is at unity in himself, desires the same objects with all parts of his soul, wishes himself what is good, and sympathises with his Self in griefs and joys; wicked men are divided, full of remorse, and cannot be friends with themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being a friend to oneself (self-sympathy, unity) is a precondition for being able to be a friend to another; the wicked lack the inner unity that grounds friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendly feelings derive from relations to one's Self
rubrics_metrics.description: People generally characterise Friendship by marks that the good man has towards himself; a friend feels towards a friend as towards himself (a friend is in fact another Self).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual link implies that criteria for friendship mirror the dispositions one has toward one's own good: wishing good for the other's sake, doing what is good for them, and sharing life/objects.
